- When sentiment is consistently positive (≥0.6) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast slope or cap upward momentum.
- When sentiment is negative (≤0.4) or volatile, model often underestimates sharp drops; add buffer for downside risk or adjust downward early.
- After a price spike (e.g., >85), model frequently overcorrects with a steep upward trend; cap forecast growth after peak or introduce lagged decay.
- If true outcome shows strong mean reversion (e.g., 30d price drops from 85+ to 75+), model often fails to reflect this; apply smoothing or decay factor to forecast.
- When sentiment is flat (0.0–0.2) or neutral, model tends to drift toward historical mean; avoid linear extrapolation; use volatility-adjusted baseline.
- For 30d forecasts, if true outcome deviates >10% from initial forecast, check sentiment for divergence — if sentiment shifts sharply, adjust forecast direction accordingly.
- If sentiment history shows recent reversal (e.g., from +0.7 to -0.4), model often misses the turn; reduce forecast slope or add early warning signal.
